title: Shelter Island Plantation Claim (1651–1652)
summary: On Manhansett homeland between Long Island’s forks, Nathaniel and Constant Sylvester, Thomas Middleton and Thomas Rouse claimed an island-wide plantation supplying Barbados. Native residents challenged threatened removal. The story connects contested land agreements, Native labor, African enslavement and continuing Indigenous relationships.

why_this_matters: A colonial land record describes a claim made at a particular time. Read its conditions and the people affected alongside the map; an outlined claim is not proof that Native relationships or rights ended.
introduction_title: Land, records and continuing Native history
introduction_content: On Manhansett homeland between Long Island’s forks, Nathaniel and Constant Sylvester, Thomas Middleton and Thomas Rouse claimed an island-wide plantation supplying Barbados. Native residents challenged threatened removal. The story connects contested land agreements, Native labor, African enslavement and continuing Indigenous relationships.
history_content:
An inhabited island, not an empty estate

Shelter Island lies between the North and South Forks of eastern Long Island. Manhansack-Ahaquatuwamock is one recorded form of its Native name. The Manhansett community had political and cultural connections with Montauk. The later plantation claim covered the island, not just the present Sylvester Manor historic property. That difference explains the broad shaded landscape on this map. Fiske Center, University of Massachusetts Boston: Sylvester Manor, Shelter Island, NY

Who claimed the land—and for which colonial interests?

James Farrett acted for William Alexander, Earl of Stirling, whose claims came through English colonization. In 1641 Farrett transferred his island claim to Stephen Goodyear, a New Haven merchant. In 1651 Goodyear sold to four Barbados sugar merchants: Thomas Middleton, Thomas Rouse, and brothers Constant and Nathaniel Sylvester. These were transfers among colonists, not evidence that Manhansett residents accepted the extent of their claims. Town of Shelter Island: History of Shelter Island

English merchants with Dutch and Caribbean connections

The Sylvesters were an English family with commercial roots in the Netherlands. Sylvester Manor describes the original business as an Anglo-Dutch consortium. Nathaniel became its resident proprietor while the partnership supplied the Barbados plantation economy. “Anglo-Dutch” describes those merchant connections; it does not turn the Manhansett homeland into unoccupied land available for a European government or company to distribute. Sylvester Manor: History and Heritage

Manhansett people challenged removal

In the commissioners’ record reproduced by Jacob Mallmann, Checkanoe spoke for the island’s Native inhabitants against Captain Middleton’s claim through Goodyear and Farrett. They said Farrett had received only an area marked by trees and that they had never agreed to lose their homes. The complaint concerns both the extent of the land and the right to remain. It is more specific than a general claim that Native people did not understand deeds. Jacob E. Mallmann: Historical Papers on Shelter Island and Its Presbyterian Church

A ceremony of possession did not make Native people disappear

A later declaration names the sachem Yokee, Captain Nathaniel Sylvester and Ensign John Booth. It describes delivery of turf and a twig using an English possession ceremony and claims the Native inhabitants departed. Its written date is March 23, 1652; Mallmann explains that the Old Style year makes this March 1653 in modern year numbering. The declaration is evidence of a colonial claim, not sufficient proof that everyone left. Jacob E. Mallmann: Historical Papers on Shelter Island and Its Presbyterian Church

How the plantation changed work and land

The partnership cleared woodland, cultivated crops and raised livestock for export. Oak became barrel staves for the sugar trade. Enslaved Africans brought through Barbados and indentured European workers supplied labor. Nathaniel Sylvester’s 1680 will names people held in bondage as family groups. Naming the proprietors alone would conceal the people whose labor made their estate possible. Sylvester Manor: Slavery at the Manor

Native presence continued within a transformed landscape

The Fiske Center’s research identifies Native labor and wampum production during the plantation’s early operation. These findings contradict a simple disappearance story. Land loss could mean continuing to live or work in a homeland while control of its fields, resources and labor passed into colonial hands. Native workers, enslaved Africans and Europeans did not occupy equal positions in that economy. Fiske Center, University of Massachusetts Boston: Sylvester Manor, Shelter Island, NY

The Pharaoh brothers: a later Native family history

In November 1829, Esther Pharaoh placed her sons William and Isaac with proprietor Samuel Smith Gardiner after their father Joseph, a Montaukett man, died. The indentures bound their labor until age twenty-one in exchange for maintenance, basic education and an eventual payment. William left in August 1840 before his term ended and joined a whaling voyage; Isaac remained. Their lives connect Shelter Island with Montaukett family history well beyond the seventeenth-century deeds. Read the fuller account at Sylvester Manor rather than treating indenture as an ordinary modern employment agreement. Sylvester Manor: The Indenture of William and Isaac Pharaoh and Their Lasting Legacy

Living relationships and responsibilities

Sylvester Manor records a project begun in 2021 with members of the Shinnecock Graves Protection Warrior Society, Honor Our Indigenous Ancestors, Unkechaug Nation and Long Island tribal descendants. That collaboration shows why the island’s history concerns living Native communities, not only a European family’s property archive. It does not establish that every participant has the same ancestry or that the historic estate has been returned to tribal ownership. This map offers historical interpretation, not directions to sensitive places or permission to enter private land. Sylvester Manor: History and Heritage
whereintheworld_content:
The source explicitly describes an island-wide plantation. The polygon therefore follows the main Shelter Island landmass in the modern shoreline mask, rather than today’s much smaller manor property. This is an approximate colonial claimed extent. It does not certify Native consent, a legal extinguishment of rights, or an unchanged 1651 shoreline. Neighboring islands and exact archaeological locations are excluded.
